1.q: You are asked to enter a tank classed as a confined space. No permit is available. What should you do first?
o: Ask a colleague if entry was allowed yesterday.
Enter briefly because the task will only take minutes.
Go in while someone watches from outside.
Refuse entry until a valid permit is issued.
Start preparing tools inside the tank.
1.w: Confined space entry should not begin without a valid permit confirming checks, controls and authorisation.

n.1: Short duration does not remove permit requirements.
n.0: Previous permissions do not replace a current permit.
n.2: Watching from outside is not enough without formal controls.
n.4: Preparing tools inside is still unauthorised entry.

1.q: A worker removes ear defenders because the task will only take two minutes. What is the best response?
o: Noise rules still apply during short tasks
Short jobs never need hearing protection
Stand farther away and ignore site rules
Use one ear defender only
Wear gloves instead
1.w: Even short exposure to high noise can be harmful.

n.1: Brief exposure can still damage hearing.
n.3: One-sided protection is usually inadequate.
n.2: Distance may help but does not override controls.
n.4: Gloves do not protect hearing.

1.q: Before using a tight-fitting respirator, what should you carry out?
o: A fit check.
A glove change.
A hearing test.
A ladder inspection.
A toolbox talk only.
1.w: A fit check helps confirm the respirator seals correctly before use.

n.2: A hearing test is unrelated to respirator fit.
n.4: A briefing does not replace checking the seal.
n.3: Ladder inspections are unrelated.
n.1: Changing gloves does not confirm respirator fit.

1.q: A van starts reversing toward a narrow gate you need to use. What is the best action?
o: Knock on the rear door
Slip through the gate before it arrives
Stand behind the van so the driver sees you
Wait outside the no-go zone until reversing is complete
Walk beside the bumper
1.w: Stay clear of the reversing area and wait until the manoeuvre is finished.

n.1: Trying to beat a reversing vehicle is unsafe.
n.2: Standing behind the van puts you in a blind spot.
n.0: Approaching a reversing vehicle increases risk.
n.4: Walking beside the bumper may place you in a crush zone.

1.q: Why is it important to report suspect asbestos immediately rather than at the end of the shift?
o: Because all suspect materials must be removed by labourers before handover
Because asbestos becomes harmless if it is reported within the same day
Because management prefers early paperwork
Because other workers may disturb it before the risk is controlled
Because the report will be cheaper to process in the morning
1.w: Immediate reporting helps prevent others from unknowingly disturbing the suspect material.

n.2: The key issue is safety, not paperwork timing.
n.4: Cost is not the reason for immediate reporting.
n.0: Labourers should not remove suspect asbestos.
n.1: Delay does not make asbestos harmless.

1.q: You are moving boxes through a doorway with a trolley. What is the best action?
o: Pull backwards without looking
Rush through before anyone arrives
Slow down and make sure the load stays stable
Stack boxes above eye level first
Tilt the trolley sharply to fit faster
1.w: Doorways need slower controlled movement and stable loading.

n.1: Rushing increases collision risk.
n.4: Sharp tilting may tip the load.
n.3: High stacking can block vision and destabilise loads.
n.0: Moving backward without looking is unsafe.

1.q: If a first alarm point fails to operate, what should you do next?
o: Assume someone else noticed
Give up and continue working
Hide the fault from management
Keep testing it for an hour
Use another method to raise the alarm and report the failure
1.w: Use an alternative alarm route immediately and report the defect.

n.1: Emergencies still require action.
n.3: Extended testing wastes time.
n.2: Concealing faults is unsafe.
n.0: Assumptions may delay response.

1.q: What is the main benefit of recycling materials on site?
o: It always costs more
It is only for large sites
It makes the site noisier
It reduces waste sent to landfill
It slows every job down
1.w: Recycling keeps usable material out of landfill and reduces the site's impact.

n.0: It often saves money.
n.1: It applies to all sites.
n.2: Recycling is unrelated to noise.
n.4: Not generally true.

1.q: A worker slips on a wet floor, catches the handrail and avoids falling. What does this indicate?
o: A first-aid incident requiring treatment
A near miss that should be reported
An equipment fault unrelated to safety
No issue because balance was recovered
Only a housekeeping matter with no reporting value
1.w: The event could have caused injury and highlights a hazard, so it is a reportable near miss.

n.3: Avoiding injury does not remove the risk.
n.4: Housekeeping hazards should still be reported when they nearly injure someone.
n.2: The main issue is slip risk, not necessarily equipment fault.
n.0: No injury means first aid is not the classification.

1.q: If a manual call point has a protective cover, what should you do in an emergency?
o: Leave it because covers mean out of use
Only use it if smoke is heavy
Operate it as designed to raise the alarm
Use it only with permission first
Wait for maintenance staff
1.w: Protective covers help prevent misuse but call points should still be used in emergencies.

n.0: A cover does not mean unusable.
n.4: Do not delay for maintenance staff.
n.1: Raise the alarm as soon as fire is discovered.
n.3: Emergency use should not wait for permission.

1.q: Which TWO reduce the danger from a reversing vehicle?
o: A reversing alarm
A trained banksman
Assuming the driver can see you
Standing directly behind it
Walking across its path
1.w: A banksman and a reversing alarm warn of and control the reversing movement.

n.2: Blind spots mean you may not be seen.
n.3: The most dangerous place to be.
n.4: Puts you in the danger zone.

1.q: You see a general warning triangle but cannot tell the exact hazard. What should you do first?
o: Cover the sign
Ignore it if others continue
Move it nearer the gate
Stop and assess the area
Take a shortcut through
1.w: If unsure, pause and identify the risk before proceeding.

n.1: Others may be mistaken or authorised differently.
n.0: Never interfere with signage.
n.4: Shortcuts can expose you to unknown hazards.
n.2: Only authorised persons reposition signs.

1.q: A forklift warning sign is posted at a blind corner. What is the best action?
o: Assume drivers will stop for you
Slow down, look and listen before crossing
Turn the sign around
Use headphones to reduce noise
Walk in the vehicle lane
1.w: The sign warns of vehicle movement, so check carefully before entering.

n.0: Never rely solely on drivers seeing you.
n.3: Headphones reduce awareness.
n.4: Vehicle lanes increase exposure risk.
n.2: Do not alter safety signage.

1.q: Which information is least useful in an emergency call?
o: Best access gate for responders
Exact site address
Number of casualties
Type of incident
What snacks are available in the canteen
1.w: Canteen snacks are irrelevant compared with incident details and access information.

n.1: Location is highly important.
n.3: Incident type helps responders prepare.
n.2: Casualty numbers are important.
n.0: Access routes can save time.

1.q: Which symptom may indicate hand-arm vibration problems?
o: Dust on your gloves.
Mud on your boots.
Numb or white fingers.
Sore knees after kneeling.
Sunburn on the neck.
1.w: Numbness or fingers turning white can be warning signs linked to vibration exposure.

n.4: This is unrelated to vibration injury.
n.3: Knee soreness is a different issue.
n.0: Dust on gloves is not a HAVS symptom.
n.1: Boot condition is unrelated.

1.q: Why can warming up be useful before manual handling work?
o: It guarantees you cannot be injured
It helps prepare muscles and joints for movement
It makes heavy loads lighter
It means technique no longer matters
It removes the need for breaks
1.w: Warming up may help readiness for physical activity and movement.

n.0: No warm-up can guarantee zero injury risk.
n.3: Safe technique always matters.
n.2: Weight of the load does not change.
n.4: Breaks may still be needed.

1.q: You notice one wheel lock on a mobile tower is broken. What should you do?
o: Chock the wheel with scrap timber
Take the tower out of use until repaired
Use it if three other locks work
Use it only for low-level tasks
Use it only indoors
1.w: Defective wheel locks can allow movement, so the tower should not be used until fixed.

n.4: Indoor use does not remove the defect.
n.2: One failed lock can still create movement risk.
n.0: Improvised chocks are unreliable.
n.3: Low height does not make defective equipment safe.

1.q: Which TWO are correct about working near overhead power lines?
o: Assume they are switched off
Raise loads higher to clear them by eye
Touch them to test
Treat all lines as live
Use goalposts and exclusion zones
1.w: Overhead lines are always treated as live, and goalposts and exclusion zones keep plant clear.

n.0: All lines are treated as live.
n.1: Judging clearance by eye is unsafe; set physical limits.
n.2: Never test a line by contact.

1.q: You hear the alarm in an outdoor work area. What should you assume?
o: It can be ignored outside
It is only a test every time
It only applies to office staff
The evacuation procedure still applies to you
You should wait for a text message
1.w: Outdoor workers should also follow the site's emergency evacuation procedure.

n.2: Emergency procedures often apply site-wide.
n.0: Being outside does not always remove danger.
n.1: Treat alarms seriously unless told otherwise.
n.4: Do not delay waiting for messages.

1.q: A load slips slightly from a forklift but nobody is hurt. What should happen?
o: Ignore it because no one was injured
Move on quickly to avoid delays
Only mention it if asked later
Report it as a near miss
Wait to see if it happens again
1.w: Near misses should be reported so causes can be investigated and future harm prevented.

n.0: No injury does not mean no serious risk existed.
n.2: Delayed reporting can lose important details.
n.4: Repeated events may lead to injury.
n.1: Productivity should not override safety reporting.

1.q: A labourer cannot read complex written instructions in English. What should the employer do?
o: Discipline them for asking questions
Expect co-workers to translate everything unofficially
Ignore the issue because papers were handed out
Move them to any task without explanation
Provide information in a form they can understand
1.w: Safety information should be communicated in a way workers can understand.

n.2: Handing out unread material may be ineffective.
n.1: Unofficial translation may be incomplete.
n.0: Questions should be encouraged, not punished.
n.3: Unexplained reassignment does not solve communication issues.

1.q: How can regular breaks help when using vibrating tools?
o: They allow longer continuous use safely.
They guarantee no injury will occur.
They make the tool vibrate more.
They reduce continuous exposure time.
They remove the need for limits.
1.w: Breaks help reduce continuous exposure and give hands time to recover.

n.2: Breaks do not increase vibration.
n.4: Exposure limits may still apply.
n.1: Breaks reduce risk but do not guarantee safety.
n.0: Breaks are not for extending unsafe continuous use.

1.q: Before workers start lifting heavy materials repeatedly, what should an employer do?
o: Assess the risk and put controls in place
Double the workload to finish sooner
Remove all rest breaks
Tell workers to manage it themselves
Wait for an injury before changing anything
1.w: Risk control starts with assessing hazards and implementing suitable measures.

n.3: Employers retain duties to manage risks.
n.4: Action should happen before injuries occur.
n.1: More workload may increase risk.
n.2: Removing breaks can worsen fatigue.

1.q: Which TWO actions are correct if you disturb a material you think may contain asbestos?
o: Break a piece off to check
Keep working carefully
Report it to your supervisor
Stop work immediately
Sweep it up quickly
1.w: Suspected asbestos means stop work and report it; never disturb it.

n.0: Disturbing suspected asbestos releases fibres.
n.1: You must stop, not continue.
n.4: Sweeping spreads fibres into the air.

1.q: Why should materials not be stacked beneath overhead lines?
o: They always rust faster
They block sunlight only
They keep getting wet
They lower fuel quality
They may reduce safe clearance and encourage access
1.w: Stored materials can reduce clearances and tempt work activity within the danger area.

n.2: Weather is not the main issue.
n.0: Rusting is not the key hazard.
n.1: Sunlight is irrelevant.
n.3: Fuel quality is unrelated.

1.q: Why is hearing loss from noise a serious risk on site?
o: It always causes back pain.
It can be permanent and gradual.
It disappears after every shift.
It improves concentration.
It only affects visitors.
1.w: Noise-induced hearing loss often develops gradually and may be permanent.

n.0: Back pain is unrelated to hearing loss.
n.4: Workers and others can be affected, not only visitors.
n.2: Hearing damage may not recover.
n.3: Hearing loss does not improve concentration.

1.q: What is the main problem with relying only on hazard tape around a deep excavation?
o: It gives warning but does not properly stop falls.
It is only suitable for marking indoor storage areas.
It makes the excavation look more dangerous than it is.
It may fade in bad weather.
It prevents emergency services from finding the excavation.
1.w: Tape can warn people, but it is not normally enough to physically prevent falls into an excavation.

n.3: Weathering may happen, but the main issue is lack of fall protection.
n.1: The issue is not that tape is only for indoor use.
n.4: Emergency access is not the main concern in this situation.
n.2: The danger is real where an excavation edge is unprotected.

1.q: What is a common use of a portable transformer on site?
o: Charging phones
Drying wet gloves
Storing extension leads
Supplying 110V tools safely from mains power
Testing ladders
1.w: Portable transformers are commonly used to supply 110V tools from mains sources on site.

n.0: Phone charging is not the main construction-site purpose.
n.4: Transformers do not test ladders.
n.1: They are not drying equipment.
n.2: They are not storage units.

1.q: A coworker keeps throwing small items across the site for fun. What is the best action?
o: Hide the items and say nothing.
Laugh and carry on working.
Move closer so you can catch them.
Tell them to stop and report it if it continues.
Throw them back.
1.w: Throwing objects is unsafe and can injure others. It should be challenged and reported if it continues.

n.4: Throwing items back escalates the risk.
n.1: Ignoring unsafe acts allows them to continue.
n.2: Moving closer increases your risk of injury.
n.0: Silence does not address the unsafe behaviour.

1.q: What equipment is normally used to supply a 110V tool from a 230V mains source?
o: Battery charger
Distribution board key
Fuse puller
Transformer
Voltage tester
1.w: A site transformer is commonly used to step down the supply for 110V tools.

n.0: A battery charger is not used to power standard 110V site tools from mains.
n.4: A voltage tester measures supply but does not provide it.
n.1: A key does not convert voltage.
n.2: A fuse puller is unrelated to voltage conversion.

1.q: Pedestrians are stepping around barriers because the temporary walkway is blocked with materials. What should happen?
o: Clear the walkway and maintain a safe signed route.
Ignore it if only a few people do it.
Leave it until deliveries are finished.
Remove the barriers completely.
Tell pedestrians to be more careful.
1.w: Walkways should be kept clear so pedestrians use the protected route instead of entering danger areas.

n.2: Delays allow unsafe behaviour to continue.
n.4: The route should be made safe, not blame pedestrians.
n.3: Removing barriers reduces protection.
n.1: Even a few people entering danger areas is unacceptable.

1.q: Why is horseplay dangerous on a construction site?
o: It can distract people and cause accidents.
It improves concentration.
It makes tools work faster.
It only affects visitors.
It reduces the need for supervision.
1.w: Horseplay can distract workers, reduce awareness and lead to injuries or incidents.

n.1: Horseplay usually reduces concentration.
n.2: It does not improve tool performance.
n.4: Supervision may become more necessary.
n.3: Anyone nearby may be affected.

1.q: Which action is an error when a driver signals you to pass but you cannot see the route fully?
o: Asking for the vehicle to stop fully
Checking both sides before moving
Refusing and waiting until safe
Using a marked crossing point
Walking through anyway because you were signalled
1.w: You should only move when you are satisfied the route is safe, not rely blindly on signals.

n.2: Waiting is acceptable if unsure.
n.1: Checking the route is good practice.
n.3: Marked crossings are preferred.
n.0: Stopping the vehicle can improve safety.

1.q: You are lifting a small toolbox from the floor. What should move first to start the lift?
o: Arms pulling upward before the legs engage
Back straightening suddenly before the legs move
Legs driving upward while the back stays straight
One foot stepping back while leaning sideways
Shoulders twisting toward the destination
1.w: The legs should provide the main lifting force while maintaining a straight back.

n.0: Arms should assist grip, not take the main load.
n.4: Twisting should be avoided.
n.1: Sudden back movement can strain tissues.
n.3: Side leaning reduces balance.

1.q: You need to reposition a mobile tower by two metres. What is the safest sequence?
o: Climb down, clear tools, unlock wheels, move, relock wheels
Move it first, then tell the worker above
Push it while standing on the platform
Tilt it onto two wheels and roll it
Unlock one wheel and drag the tower sideways
1.w: The tower should be vacated, made clear, moved safely, then wheels relocked before use.

n.2: Occupied movement is unsafe.
n.4: Partial unlocking and dragging can destabilise the tower.
n.1: No one should remain above during movement.
n.3: Tilting the tower can cause loss of control.

1.q: Which action is an error when using pedestrian walkways?
o: Following one-way pedestrian signs
Keeping inside the marked route
Reporting obstructions on the path
Stepping into the vehicle route to avoid a puddle
Watching for plant at crossings
1.w: Leaving the walkway and stepping into traffic to avoid a puddle creates unnecessary danger.

n.1: Staying within the route is correct practice.
n.4: Awareness at crossings is sensible.
n.0: Following route signs helps safe movement.
n.2: Reporting obstructions improves route safety.

1.q: Which is an early sign of cement dermatitis?
o: Back strain
Blue nails
Dizziness only
Dry, itchy or cracked skin
Sharp tooth pain
1.w: Dryness, itching and cracking are common dermatitis signs.

n.1: This is not a typical cement dermatitis sign.
n.4: Unrelated symptom.
n.2: Not the usual skin sign.
n.0: Unrelated condition.

1.q: What should you do if your goggles fog up while using equipment?
o: Ignore it and keep working blind
Lift them onto your forehead while cutting
Spray paint on the lenses
Stop safely and clean or adjust them
Take them off for better airflow
1.w: If visibility is affected, stop safely and correct the issue before continuing.

n.1: Forehead position gives no eye protection.
n.0: Poor visibility increases risk.
n.4: Removing protection exposes the eyes.
n.2: Paint would worsen visibility.

1.q: Why should filters be changed as recommended by the manufacturer or site rules?
o: It guarantees no other controls are needed.
It increases boot grip on wet ground.
It makes the respirator look newer.
It removes the need for fit checks.
Old filters may clog or lose effectiveness.
1.w: Used filters can clog or become less effective, reducing protection.

n.2: Appearance is not the safety reason.
n.0: Other controls may still be required.
n.1: Filters do not affect footwear grip.
n.3: Fit checks are still necessary.

1.q: Which action best supports recycling on site?
o: Break containers so no one reuses them.
Ignore labels if the skip is half empty.
Keep reusable and recyclable materials separated.
Mix timber, plastic and metal together.
Put everything into one large skip.
1.w: Separating reusable and recyclable materials helps recovery and reduces waste sent for disposal.

n.3: Mixing streams can reduce recycling value.
n.4: Single mixed skips usually reduce recovery rates.
n.1: Labels should still be followed.
n.0: Preventing reuse works against waste reduction.

1.q: A scaffold has ice on the boards during winter. What is the best action?
o: Scatter loose bricks for grip
Treat it as unsafe until surfaces are made safe
Use it only for urgent tasks
Use the outer edge where ice looks thinner
Walk carefully and keep one hand on the rail
1.w: Ice creates slip hazards and the platform should be made safe before use.

n.4: Careful walking does not remove slip risk.
n.2: Urgency does not justify unsafe conditions.
n.0: Loose materials create further hazards.
n.3: Outer edges can be more dangerous.

1.q: Bricklayers are working above a busy path. What should be done first?
o: Ask people to hurry through the path
Close the area below
Only issue a verbal warning from above
Tell workers below to look up while walking
Wait to see if anything falls first
1.w: Closing the area below removes people from the danger zone before objects can fall.

n.0: Moving quickly through the area still leaves people exposed.
n.4: Waiting allows unnecessary risk to continue.
n.3: Looking up does not stop falling materials striking workers.
n.2: Verbal warnings are unreliable and not a proper control.

1.q: Why do workers have legal duties under health and safety law?
o: To approve all subcontractor training records
To personally inspect every machine on site
To replace supervisors on busy days
To take reasonable care for themselves and others
To write company safety policy each week
1.w: Workers must take reasonable care for their own safety and that of others affected by their actions.

n.1: Formal inspections are usually assigned roles, not every worker.
n.2: Supervisory duties are separate responsibilities.
n.4: Policy writing is a management function.
n.0: Training record approval is not a general worker duty.

1.q: What should happen after a temporary opening in excavation fencing has been used?
o: Ask workers nearby to remember that the gap is there.
Leave it open for the next person.
Move the barrier further from the excavation so access is easier.
Put the warning sign back at the end of the day.
Re-secure it.
1.w: Temporary openings should be re-secured immediately after use to restore protection against falls.

n.1: Leaving it open creates an avoidable fall risk.
n.3: Waiting until the end of the day leaves the hazard uncontrolled.
n.0: Relying on memory is not a safe control.
n.2: Moving protection away may make it easier for people to enter the danger zone.

1.q: During evacuation, a coworker wants to use the goods lift. What should you do?
o: Agree if it is quicker
Direct them to the stairs and fire exit route
Send tools down first
Use the lift together
Wait for lift instructions
1.w: Lifts should not normally be used in fire evacuation unless specifically designated.

n.0: Speed does not make lift use safe in a fire.
n.3: Using the lift increases risk.
n.2: Tools are not the priority.
n.4: Move to the safe exit route instead of waiting.

1.q: Which TWO reduce the risk of an excavation collapsing?
o: Digging deeper quickly
Keeping spoil back from the edge
Parking plant at the edge
Removing the trench box
Shoring or battering the sides
1.w: Support and keeping loads back from the edge prevent excavation collapse.

n.0: Increases risk without support.
n.2: Loads at the edge can cause collapse.
n.3: Removes the very protection needed.

1.q: What should happen to different types of site waste?
o: They should all go in one skip
They should be buried on site
They should be burned together
They should be left in a pile
They should be segregated into separate skips
1.w: Segregating waste allows recycling and correct disposal of each type.

n.0: Mixing waste prevents recycling.
n.1: Illegal disposal.
n.2: Burning causes pollution.
n.3: Creates hazards and pollution.

1.q: You notice two similar tins, one labelled and one unlabelled. Which should be used?
o: Either if wearing gloves
Mix both together
Only the clearly labelled tin with correct instructions
The older tin first
The unlabelled tin if nearly full
1.w: Only clearly identified products with readable instructions should be used.

n.4: Quantity does not identify hazards.
n.0: PPE does not replace identification.
n.3: Age does not confirm safety.
n.1: Mixing unknown substances is dangerous.

1.q: A kettle socket catches fire in the canteen. Which extinguisher is the wrong choice because of added shock risk?
o: CO2
Dry powder
Isolate power then CO2
Water
Water mist approved for electrical use
1.w: Standard water extinguishers should not be used on live electrical fires because of shock risk.

n.0: CO2 is a common choice for electrical equipment fires.
n.1: Dry powder may be used depending site policy and equipment.
n.4: Approved water mist units can be suitable where specifically rated.
n.2: Isolating power first can make the situation safer before using a suitable extinguisher.

1.q: Which TWO are good practice for a load that is too heavy to lift alone?
o: Drag it while twisting
Get help for a team lift
Lift it quickly on your own
Throw it into place
Use a mechanical aid
1.w: A team lift or a mechanical aid removes the strain of a heavy load.

n.0: Twisting under load causes injury.
n.2: Speed does not make a heavy load safe.
n.3: Loses control of the load.

2.q: You discover flames in a plant room. What is the safest first sequence?
o: Fetch belongings, then check fire size
Film the fire, then call later
Open doors, then investigate closely
Raise alarm, warn others, leave area
Wait for someone senior first
2.w: Immediate warning and evacuation actions should come before anything else.

n.0: Belongings are not a priority.
n.2: Opening doors may worsen conditions.
n.1: Recording events delays emergency response.
n.4: Waiting wastes critical time.

2.q: Why are clean toilet facilities important on a construction site?
o: They allow waste to be stored.
They reduce the need for supervision.
They remove the need for cleaning staff.
They replace rest breaks completely.
They support hygiene, health and welfare.
2.w: Clean toilets are a basic welfare requirement that supports hygiene and worker wellbeing.

n.1: Toilets are not provided to reduce supervision.
n.3: Rest breaks are still needed.
n.2: Facilities still need cleaning and maintenance.
n.0: Toilets are not waste storage areas.

2.q: Which TWO extinguisher types are suitable for an electrical fire?
o: CO2
Dry powder
Foam
Water
Wet chemical
2.w: CO2 and dry powder can be used on electrical fires; water-based types cannot.

n.2: Foam is water-based and unsuitable for electrical fires.
n.3: Water conducts electricity and is dangerous on electrical fires.
n.4: Designed for cooking-oil fires, not electrical.

2.q: Which action is poor practice after a serious accident?
o: Calling emergency services if needed
Helping injured persons if safe
Informing management promptly
Keeping people away from danger
Moving tools and materials unnecessarily before investigation
2.w: Unnecessary disturbance of the scene can interfere with investigation.

n.0: Emergency contact may be essential.
n.3: Controlling access is sensible.
n.2: Prompt notification is good practice.
n.1: Safe assistance to casualties is appropriate.

2.q: Workers need temporary access through excavation fencing. What is the safest approach?
o: Leave a gap open.
Let each worker decide the safest place to enter.
Remove the warning signs while the access route is being used.
Take down the full fence line so there is more room.
Use controlled access.
2.w: Temporary access should be controlled, limited, and protected so the excavation edge is not left exposed.

n.0: An open gap creates an uncontrolled fall risk.
n.3: Removing the full fence line exposes more of the excavation.
n.2: Warning signs should remain where they are needed.
n.1: Access points should be planned, not chosen individually.

2.q: Why is hearing protection important in noisy work areas?
o: It guarantees tools will run more quietly
It helps reduce the risk of permanent hearing damage
It makes machines use less fuel
It removes the need for supervision
It replaces eye protection
2.w: Repeated exposure to high noise can cause lasting hearing loss or tinnitus.

n.0: Hearing PPE protects the worker, not the machine noise output.
n.3: Supervision and controls are still required.
n.2: Fuel use is unrelated.
n.4: Different PPE protects different hazards.

2.q: A labourer trips over a loose cable but regains balance and is not injured. What should happen next?
o: Ignore it because no one was hurt
Move the cable later if there is time
Only mention it at the next toolbox talk
Report the near miss so the hazard can be corrected
Wait to see if someone else trips first
2.w: A near miss should be reported promptly so the hazard can be removed before it causes an injury.

n.0: No injury does not remove the duty to report a near miss.
n.4: Waiting increases the chance of an actual accident.
n.1: Delaying action leaves the risk in place.
n.2: Formal reporting should not be delayed until a later meeting.

2.q: You are guiding a telehandler. The driver loses sight of you. What should happen next?
o: Ask another worker to shout directions
Continue using hand signals from the side
Run to the front of the machine
Stand nearer the wheels
The driver should stop until sight is regained
2.w: If the driver loses sight of the banksman or guide, operations should stop until visibility is restored.

n.1: Signals are ineffective if the driver cannot see you.
n.2: Running in front increases danger.
n.3: Standing near wheels creates crush risk.
n.0: Shouted directions are unreliable and unsafe.

2.q: Why are barriers used around openings during temporary work?
o: To dry wet concrete faster
To improve lighting levels
To increase floor space
To make covers lighter
To stop access into a fall hazard area
2.w: Barriers restrict access and warn workers away from dangerous openings.

n.1: Lighting is not the main purpose.
n.3: They do not affect cover weight.
n.2: They do not create floor space.
n.0: They do not dry concrete.

2.q: You find the cable sheath worn through near the plug but no copper is visible yet. What should you do?
o: Bend the cable the other way and continue
Keep checking it during the day
Only use it on 110V tools
Stop using it and report the damage before it worsens
Use it if you wear gloves
2.w: Damage to the outer sheath is enough to take the lead out of service and report it before conductors become exposed.

n.1: Monitoring a damaged cable is not enough once a defect is found.
n.2: Lower voltage does not make damaged equipment acceptable to use.
n.4: Gloves do not remove the defect or the site risk.
n.0: Repositioning the cable does not repair the damage.

2.q: What ladder angle is generally regarded as safest for a leaning ladder?
o: About 45 degrees so it feels stable
About 75 degrees, roughly 1 out for every 4 up
Almost vertical with the feet close in
Any angle if someone holds the ladder
As shallow as possible to reduce height
2.w: The common guide is a 1:4 ratio, giving an angle of about 75 degrees.

n.0: Too shallow increases the chance of the ladder slipping out.
n.2: Too steep increases the chance of tipping backwards.
n.3: Holding a ladder does not replace correct positioning.
n.4: Very shallow angles are unstable.

2.q: You are asked to use a trolley to move blocks across site. One wheel is loose and wobbles badly. What should you do?
o: Ask a workmate to steady the load while moving
Carry more blocks so fewer trips are needed
Report the defect and use another safe trolley if available
Use it only on smooth ground
Use it slowly for one trip only
2.w: Workers should use equipment properly and report defective equipment before use.

n.4: A single trip with defective equipment can still cause injury.
n.0: Extra help does not remove the defect.
n.1: Increasing the load may worsen the risk.
n.3: Surface condition does not fix the faulty wheel.

2.q: Which TWO should always be reported?
o: A near miss
A perfect day with no issues
A tidy welfare area
An injury needing first aid
Finishing early
2.w: Near misses and injuries are both reported so risks can be acted on.

n.1: Nothing to report.
n.2: Good, but not a reportable event.
n.4: Not a safety matter.

2.q: What should you do if your visitor loses their temporary badge on site?
o: Ignore it until they leave
Lend them your own badge
Report it immediately and follow site instructions
Tell them to hide from security
Write one on paper yourself
2.w: Lost badges affect access control and should be reported promptly.

n.0: Delay weakens site security and records.
n.1: Sharing badges is improper.
n.4: Unauthorised homemade badges are unacceptable.
n.3: Avoiding security is not a valid solution.

2.q: Which TWO tell you how to handle a hazardous product safely?
o: The brand name
The colour of the container
The price
The product label
The safety data sheet
2.w: The label and the safety data sheet give the safe-handling information.

n.0: Does not tell you the hazards.
n.1: Colour is not a reliable guide.
n.2: Irrelevant to safe handling.

2.q: Your boot laces snap and the boot feels loose. What should you do first?
o: Ignore it if the toe cap is sound
Replace or secure the laces properly
Tuck loose ends inside the boot
Use one lace across both boots
Walk more slowly for the shift
2.w: Loose footwear increases trip risk and reduces support.

n.2: Unsecured boots can still slip or trip you.
n.4: Walking slower does not solve the defect.
n.3: Improvised lacing may not hold safely.
n.0: Toe protection alone is not enough.

2.q: What is the correct action if muddy water is running off site onto the road?
o: Cover it with more soil
Ignore it as normal
Let it dry on the road
Stop it at source and clean the road
Wash it into the surface drain
2.w: Run-off is controlled at source and any mud on the public road is cleaned up promptly.

n.0: Makes it worse.
n.1: Mud on the road is a hazard and nuisance.
n.2: Leaves mud and a hazard.
n.4: Pollutes the watercourse.

2.q: Your boot tread is almost smooth. What risk increases most?
o: Difficulty signing into the site office
Extra noise while walking slowly
Loss of hearing protection nearby
Slipping on wet or contaminated surfaces
Sunburn on exposed ankles during work
2.w: Worn tread reduces grip, especially on wet ground.

n.4: Tread wear does not cause sunburn.
n.0: Site access is unrelated to tread.
n.1: Noise is not the key safety issue.
n.2: Boot tread does not affect hearing PPE.

2.q: You see a small fire involving petrol spilled beside a generator. Which extinguisher should you use first?
o: Class D powder
Foam
Water
Water mist
Wet chemical
2.w: Foam is commonly used on flammable liquid fires such as petrol because it helps smother the surface and prevent re-ignition.

n.2: Water can spread burning liquid and increase the fire risk.
n.4: Wet chemical is mainly intended for cooking oil and fat fires.
n.3: Water mist may be suitable in some settings but foam is the standard best choice here.
n.0: Class D powder is intended for combustible metal fires.

2.q: What should you do if cable plans are unclear or missing?
o: Dig faster to reduce time exposed
Guess where services are and start carefully
Ignore plans and rely only on luck
Stop and obtain proper information before digging
Use the largest bucket available
2.w: If plans are unclear or unavailable, work should not proceed until proper information is obtained.

n.1: Guessing buried service locations is unsafe.
n.4: Large buckets increase strike risk.
n.0: Speed does not remove uncertainty.
n.2: Luck is not a control measure.

2.q: Which mechanical aid is usually best for moving loose materials such as rubble or soil?
o: Ladder platform
Office trolley
Pallet truck
Step stool
Wheelbarrow
2.w: A wheelbarrow is designed for loose materials and uneven site conditions.

n.2: Pallet trucks are for palletised loads on firm surfaces.
n.1: Office trolleys are unsuitable for site rubble.
n.0: A ladder platform is not for transporting loads.
n.3: A step stool is not a transport aid.

2.q: Work is taking place beside a busy footpath. What should be provided first to protect pedestrians?
o: A worker shouting warnings when people pass.
Loose tape tied between cones.
Nothing if the job is short.
Open access so people can choose their route.
Secure barriers separating the public from the work area.
2.w: Physical barriers help separate pedestrians from site hazards and are a key public protection measure.

n.0: Shouting warnings is unreliable and does not provide separation.
n.1: Loose tape may be inadequate in busy public areas.
n.2: Short duration does not remove the need for protection.
n.3: Uncontrolled access exposes pedestrians to risk.

2.q: Why should pedestrian walkways around site works be clearly marked?
o: To guide the public safely past hazards.
To increase vehicle speeds nearby.
To remove the need for lighting.
To replace all fencing requirements.
To slow people down for no reason.
2.w: Clearly marked walkways help direct pedestrians away from hazards and through safe routes.

n.4: The purpose is safety, not delay.
n.1: Walkways are not for increasing traffic speed.
n.3: Fencing may still be needed.
n.2: Lighting may still be necessary.

2.q: A loading shovel is parked with engine running. What is the best action before passing nearby?
o: Assume it will stay still and pass behind
Climb onto the step to ask permission
Pass under the raised arm
Wait for operator acknowledgement or use another safe route
Walk close to the bucket
2.w: Running plant may move unexpectedly, so ensure the operator knows you are there or avoid the area.

n.0: Assumptions around running plant are unsafe.
n.1: Climbing onto plant without authorisation is unsafe.
n.4: Attachments are danger zones.
n.2: Never pass under raised equipment.

2.q: Which statement best describes a worker's legal duty if their actions could affect others?
o: They are only responsible for their own safety
They are responsible only when supervised
They can ignore others if they are subcontractors
They must work in a way that does not put others at risk
They only need to act safely after an accident
2.w: Worker duties extend to others who may be affected by their acts or omissions.

n.0: Duties are wider than personal safety alone.
n.1: Responsibilities apply whether supervised or not.
n.2: Others on site must also be considered.
n.4: Safety duties apply before incidents occur.

2.q: A section of fencing has fallen, leaving direct access from the pavement into the site. What is the best action?
o: Assume nobody will enter.
Put tools in front of the gap.
Reinstate protection or secure the area immediately and report it.
Stand nearby if you have time.
Wait until the next inspection.
2.w: Broken fencing creating public access should be secured promptly and reported.

n.4: Delay leaves the public exposed to risk.
n.3: Standing nearby is not reliable protection.
n.1: Loose tools are not suitable barriers.
n.0: You should not rely on assumptions where access exists.

2.q: A co-worker says a material cannot be asbestos because it looks too modern. What is the best response?
o: Agree and continue because appearance is enough
Ask him to break some off so you can both judge it better
Carry on this time and make a note to ask someone later if there is time
Explain that you cannot rely on appearance alone and the material should be checked
Ignore the concern because asbestos is only found in pipe lagging
2.w: You cannot identify asbestos safely by appearance alone, so suspect materials should be checked properly.

n.0: Visual guesswork is unreliable and unsafe.
n.1: Breaking the material can release fibres.
n.4: Asbestos can be found in more than just pipe lagging.
n.2: Delaying action still leaves people exposed to risk.

2.q: You see a trip hazard warning near stacked materials blocking a walkway. What does the sign most likely relate to?
o: Drinking water point
Fire point location
Need for face fit testing
Obstructions causing falls
Radiation exposure
2.w: Trip warnings usually relate to obstructions, uneven ground or similar hazards.

n.2: Respiratory controls are unrelated.
n.4: Radiation uses specific symbols.
n.1: Fire points use red signage.
n.0: Water points are informational.

2.q: You see a barrier removed from an open edge to allow materials through. What should you do?
o: Ensure protection is reinstated immediately after use
Ignore it if no one is nearby
Leave it open if the task is quick
Use tape on the floor only
Wait until the end of the shift
2.w: Temporary removal should be tightly controlled and protection restored straight away.

n.2: Short duration does not remove the fall risk.
n.1: Someone may approach unexpectedly.
n.3: Floor tape alone is not adequate edge protection.
n.4: Delaying reinstatement leaves workers exposed.

2.q: You are lifting on wet ground. What matters most before starting?
o: Keeping feet close together
Leaning backward as you rise
Lifting quickly before you slip
Making sure your footing is secure and stable
Pulling mostly with your arms
2.w: Secure footing is essential to maintain balance and control.

n.2: Speed does not replace safe footing.
n.0: Feet close together reduces stability.
n.4: Arms should not take the main load.
n.1: Leaning backward may cause imbalance.

2.q: Which statement about locating first aid arrangements is correct?
o: It changes daily so there is no point learning it
Only managers need that information
Workers should find out by guessing
You only need to know after an injury happens
You should know them from induction or early in the job
2.w: Workers should know first-aid arrangements before incidents occur.

n.3: Waiting until an injury wastes time.
n.1: All workers benefit from knowing arrangements.
n.0: Even if arrangements change, they should still be communicated.
n.2: Guessing is unreliable and unsafe.

2.q: What is the main reason to use a trolley for multiple boxes?
o: It allows unsafe stacking safely
It makes every load lighter in weight
It means route checks are unnecessary
It reduces repeated lifting and carrying strain
It removes the need to steer carefully
2.w: Trolleys reduce the need to repeatedly lift and carry boxes by hand.

n.1: The weight does not change, only how it is moved.
n.4: You still need control and steering.
n.0: Unsafe stacking remains unsafe.
n.2: Routes should still be checked for hazards.

2.q: Which TWO should you do before starting a task you have not done before?
o: Ask for the method statement
Check you have the right training
Copy whoever is nearest
Guess how it is done
Start and see how it goes
2.w: Understand the method and check you are trained before starting.

n.2: They may be doing it wrong.
n.3: Guessing on an unfamiliar task is dangerous.
n.4: Never start an unknown task blind.

2.q: What should you do if you notice scaffold ties appear loose or missing?
o: Ignore it if the boards feel solid
Keep off it and report immediately
Tighten them yourself if you have a spanner
Use it only on calm days
Work only on the side nearest the building
2.w: Ties help stabilise the scaffold. Missing or loose ties can be serious defects requiring immediate reporting.

n.3: Weather does not remove the defect.
n.4: One side may still be unsafe.
n.2: Only authorised competent persons should alter scaffold components.
n.0: Solid boards do not confirm overall stability.

2.q: How should upright gas cylinders normally be secured when in use?
o: Balanced against a wall loosely
Chained or otherwise secured upright
Laid flat near the torch
Left free-standing for movement
Stacked in pairs
2.w: Cylinders should be secured upright to prevent falling and valve damage.

n.3: Unsecured cylinders can fall.
n.2: Laying cylinders flat may be unsafe depending type and setup.
n.0: Leaning loosely is unstable.
n.4: Stacking cylinders is unsafe.

2.q: You are about to use a very noisy cut-off saw. What should you do first?
o: Ignore the noise for short jobs.
Stand farther away while cutting.
Start quickly before others arrive.
Use cotton wool instead.
Wear suitable hearing protection.
2.w: Noisy tools can damage hearing, so suitable hearing protection should be worn before use.

n.2: Starting quickly does not reduce hearing risk.
n.3: Cotton wool is not suitable hearing protection.
n.0: Short exposure can still contribute to damage.
n.1: Distance alone may not provide enough protection while operating the tool.

2.q: You are carrying materials and approach a slip warning sign on a muddy ramp. Best action?
o: Drag materials sideways quickly
Keep same pace and hope for grip
Look only at the load
Reduce load or get help before using ramp
Run to maintain balance
2.w: Reduce manual handling difficulty and keep control on slippery ground.

n.1: Maintaining pace does not reduce slip risk.
n.4: Running increases loss of control.
n.2: You need to watch footing and surroundings.
n.0: Rushing with awkward movement is unsafe.

2.q: Why must you keep welfare facilities clean?
o: Because it looks good only
So they can be locked
To pass the time
To protect health and hygiene
To save water
2.w: Clean welfare facilities protect the health and hygiene of everyone using them.

n.0: The real point is hygiene.
n.1: Unrelated.
n.2: Not the reason.
n.4: Not the main reason.

2.q: A dust extractor is available for a cutting task, but setting it up takes longer. What should you do?
o: Ask others to stand back and cut dry
Open a window instead and continue
Skip it for the first few cuts
Use it only if the supervisor is nearby
Use the extractor as required for the task
2.w: Control measures provided for safe work should be used properly.

n.2: Initial cuts can still create harmful dust.
n.3: Controls apply whether supervised or not.
n.1: Ventilation alone may be insufficient.
n.0: Distance does not adequately control dust exposure.

2.q: Your boot sole is peeling away from the upper. What is the best action?
o: Ignore it until the sole fully comes off
Only wear them on dry surfaces
Replace the boots before carrying on
Swap them to the opposite feet
Tape the edge and use them this week
2.w: Separated soles reduce grip, stability and overall protection.

n.4: Temporary tape is not a reliable repair.
n.1: The defect remains on any surface.
n.3: Changing feet does not fix damage.
n.0: Defective PPE should be addressed promptly.

2.q: Why are overhead power lines dangerous even without touching them directly?
o: Electricity can arc across gaps
They always drop tools
They are weak in wind
They attract vehicles only
They make engines stall
2.w: Electricity can jump through the air and arc to nearby objects or plant.

n.1: Falling tools are not the main hazard.
n.3: They do not only affect vehicles.
n.2: Structural weakness is not the key risk here.
n.4: Engine stalling is unrelated.

2.q: Why should nearby workers be kept away from dusty cutting zones?
o: To give the operator an audience
To improve battery charging
To prevent unnecessary dust exposure
To protect wall paint only
To reduce tool noise complaints only
2.w: Exclusion zones help prevent others inhaling dust they do not need to be exposed to.

n.4: Noise may matter, but dust exposure is the key issue here.
n.0: Crowding increases risk.
n.1: Battery charging is unrelated.
n.3: Health protection is the main reason.

2.q: You discover smoke coming from a welfare cabin and no alarm has sounded. What should you do first?
o: Finish your task then report it
Look for a supervisor before acting
Move your vehicle closer
Open the door to check inside
Raise the alarm using the nearest call point
2.w: Raise the alarm immediately so others can evacuate and emergency procedures can start.

n.3: Opening doors may feed the fire or expose you to smoke.
n.0: Any delay increases danger.
n.2: Vehicle movement is not the first priority.
n.1: Do not delay alarm activation while searching for management.

2.q: Which is an error when storing labelled chemicals?
o: Checking containers for leaks
Keeping lids secure
Removing labels because you know the contents
Separating incompatible products
Using designated storage
2.w: Labels must remain in place so anyone handling the product knows the hazards.

n.1: Secure lids are good practice.
n.3: Separating incompatible products is correct.
n.4: Designated storage is correct.
n.0: Leak checks are good practice.

2.q: Which sign most strongly suggests a trench collapse risk?
o: A ladder tied in place
Clean tools nearby
Cracks appearing near the trench edge
Fresh paint on barriers
Workers wearing hi-vis clothing
2.w: Cracks near the edge may indicate ground movement and possible collapse.

n.3: Barrier paint does not indicate soil instability.
n.0: A tied ladder is normally a positive control.
n.4: PPE does not indicate trench stability.
n.1: Clean tools are unrelated.

2.q: Which action is an error on a shared traffic route?
o: Making eye contact with drivers before crossing
Reporting damaged barriers
Using marked walkways where provided
Waiting for a vehicle to pass first
Walking while distracted on your phone near moving plant
2.w: Distraction near moving vehicles reduces awareness and reaction time.

n.2: Using marked routes is correct practice.
n.0: Eye contact can help confirm awareness.
n.3: Waiting is often the safer option.
n.1: Reporting defects improves safety.

2.q: Why should spill kits be easy to access near fuel storage areas?
o: So fewer people need training.
So fuel can be stored inside them.
So spills can be tackled quickly if one happens.
So they can be borrowed for cleaning jobs.
So they stay out of sight.
2.w: Fast access helps reduce the spread and impact of accidental spills.

n.3: Spill kits are not for general cleaning use.
n.4: Hidden kits may delay response.
n.0: Training may still be needed.
n.1: Spill kits are not fuel stores.

2.q: Which TWO describe a prohibition safety sign?
o: Green background
Red border with a cross-bar
Round shape
Tells you what you must not do
Yellow triangle
2.w: A prohibition sign is round with a red border and cross-bar.

n.0: Green signs show safe conditions.
n.3: True of its meaning, but the shape/colour are the two identifying features asked for.
n.4: That is a warning sign.

2.q: Why should topsoil be stored separately during groundworks?
o: Because it is worthless
It does not matter where it goes
So it can be burned
So it can be reused and keeps its quality
To make the site look tidy only
2.w: Kept separate, topsoil retains its structure and can be reused rather than wasted.

n.0: Topsoil is a valuable resource.
n.1: Mixing spoils its quality.
n.2: Soil is not burned.
n.4: The real reason is reuse.

2.q: A trench has been dug and heavy rain starts. What is the best action?
o: Carry on because the trench is already open
Move spoil heaps closer to stop runoff
Remove the ladder to keep it dry
Stop work and have the trench condition reassessed
Work faster before it fills
2.w: Rain can weaken trench sides and increase collapse risk, so reassessment is needed.

n.0: Weather can change trench safety conditions quickly.
n.4: Speed does not remove collapse risk.
n.1: Moving spoil closer increases loading at the edge.
n.2: Removing access makes escape harder.
